title: Computational irreducibility puts permanent limits on scientific prediction

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Computational irreducibility puts permanent limits on scientific prediction

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: The Principle of Computational Equivalence and computational irreducibility show that science will never predict everything: even if the universe follows simple rules, there is in general no way to know all their consequences except by watching them unfold.

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. 12: The Principle of Computational Equivalence

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: But the Principle of Computational Equivalence—and the phenomenon of computational irreducibility—now shows that this will never happen.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci A New Kind of Science claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Stephen Wolfram, A New Kind of Science (Champaign, IL: Wolfram Media, 2002), Chapter 12, “The Principle of Computational Equivalence”; section “Historical Perspectives” (from p. 844), p. 846. Scope: science and knowledge in general

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on wolfram2002-ch12-57: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.49

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Existing proofs can establish strict predictive limits for particular universal or undecidable formal systems. The extrapolation to science and the universe requires empirical model identification and overstates what those formal results alone resolve.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: For explicitly modeled system classes, prove prediction undecidable or asymptotically as costly as evolution for specified observables, and search for counterexample predictors. Such proofs establish permanent limits for those classes; they do not show that the actual universe instantiates the required models or that every scientifically relevant observable is hard.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
The universe's exact rules and initial state are unknown.

Hardness of some predictions does not imply inability to predict everything scientifically relevant.

Simulation cannot establish permanent impossibility.

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The conditional limit is the emulation argument already available for universal cellular automata: a system that can emulate its predictor cannot be systematically outrun. The sentence applies that limit to science as such, which requires the systems science studies, or the universe, to be irreducible in this strong sense. Nothing now public establishes that physical hypothesis, and a run of successful predictions leaves a claim about everything undecided.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: If the dynamics under study are a universal computation, no predictor that is itself an effective process computes every consequence faster than the system produces them. A universality proof discharges that conditional for systems such as rule 110. An explicit shortcut for all consequences of our universe's rules would refute the application to science, and no such pair of rules and shortcut is in hand.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
The outrunning argument applies to universal systems, and whether the universe is one is open.

A claim that science never predicts everything has no finite observational cutoff.

Success on reducible questions is compatible with a permanent limit and with the absence of one.
